extracted.subtask_description: A student-facing overview that defines prose and verse, lists their types (e.g., fictional prose, free verse, blank verse), compares their structural and language features, and gives examples (including Shakespeare and a blank-verse excerpt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose refers to a kind of general creative writing; the term comes from Latin 'prosa oratio' indicating straightforward. It has uses in both fictional and nonfictional work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prose is written in words forming sentences and paragraphs; it is used in novels, short stories, scripts and other narrative forms. The article links prose to ordinary speech and grammatical correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictional prose (type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fictional prose includes novels and short stories and 'comes with a plot, setting, characters, and dialogues.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A combination of such content with emotive language works well. Example contexts: novels, short stories, dramatic scripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonfictional prose (type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonfictional prose includes factual events or information; any literary composition based on a true story is nonfictional prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to convey factual accounts and information rather than invented plots or characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroic prose (type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroic prose is present for recitation and recounts stories of heroes and legends; termed narrative prose tales composed in a dramatic style (example: islander sagas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This type is often dramatic and intended for oral or performative contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose poetry (hybrid form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose poetry is a unique form written in a rhythm or rhyme pattern and uses intensive figurative language — a combination of both prose and poetry focused on the emotional aspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It blends prose's sentence/paragraph structure with poetry's figurative and rhythmic devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Verse
rubrics_metrics.description: A verse is one-line poetry that has a definite rhyme and often uses metrical rhythm; a group of verses together is called a stanza.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verse is described as a conventional form for cultural expression, using metrical English techniques and commonly found in more 'romantic' language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free verse (type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Free verse is poetry that does not contain a rhyme scheme and whose metrical patterns vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free verse allows free play of artistic use of sound, imagery, and many literary devices; emphasis on artistic flexibility rather than fixed meter or rhyme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blank verse (type / definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Blank verse is unrhymed iambic pentameter: a consistent meter with ten syllables per line where unstressed syllables alternate with stressed syllables (five stressed syllables per line).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes blank verse 'contains iambic pentameter' and gives an example from Christopher Marlowe's Dr. Faustus. It also (in one place) describes it as 'unrhythmical' and 'focuses on passionate events' — the core technical definition is unrhymed iambic pentameter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key structural difference: sentences/paragraphs vs lines/stanzas
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose is composed of sentences that form paragraphs; verse is composed of organized lines that form stanzas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes that prose organizes ideas into sentences and paragraphs (structure of narration), whereas poetry groups lines into stanzas and multiple stanzas form a poem. It also mentions considerations like word count and sentence length as important for prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrical arrangement and rhyme as distinguishing criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose contains nonmetrical writing while verse has a metrical arrangement in sequence; verse often has definite rhyme and rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article repeatedly contrasts nonmetrical prose with the metrical nature of verse and notes verse's use of meter and rhyme schemes (except in free verse). Note: one passage on the page contains an apparent contradiction about rhyme presence; the main explanatory thread treats meter/rhyme as verse features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language/register: ordinary speech vs figurative rhythmic language
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose is preferably composed in language used in ordinary speech and sounds more natural; verse uses figurative speech and rhythmical language in each line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prose favors grammatically correct sentences and natural register; verse emphasizes figurative language and rhythmic or musical qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship/role distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: An author or writer writes prose; poets create verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a descriptive distinction of roles/labels rather than a prescriptive rule; it clarifies conventional naming: novelists/essayists = authors, poets = poets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prose vs verse in drama (Shakespearean practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare selectively uses rhymed verse and prose within his dramas; his plays contain both elements (e.g., use of blank verse alongside prose).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article points out that Shakespeare's works show selective usage (and compares prose vs verse translations such as Beowulf). The guidance implies that writers choose between prose and verse for dramatic effect and variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional advantages of prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose conveys ideas, delivers information, and combines storytelling elements (settings, plot, payoff) in a way suited to essays, stories, and commercial content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FAQ-style section lists benefits of prose: it conveys ideas, delivers information, and supports narrative structure; notes prose is more commonly used in everyday and commercial writing.
